To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) a patient who had a kidney transplant developed antibodies to donor complement binding epitopes; 2) donor epitopes were identified in the patient; and 3) donor epitopes in the patient were shared with other patients who received kidneys from the same donor.
the donor epitope sharing complement-binding antibodies were detected in the recipient serum.
the patient had a complement-binding donor-specific anti-HLA antibody (DSA) that shared a donor epitope with a non-complement-binding DSA that was present before transplantation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of complement-binding donor epitope-sharing antibodies in kidney transplant recipients.
the identification of the complement-binding donor epitope in a kidney transplant patient.
the study of the binding of the complement system to the donor HLA antigens.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the patient's serum contains a complement-binding donor HLA class II epitope sharing antibody.
the donor HLA class I epitopes shared with the recipient are the most important in terms of the development of DSA.
there is no evidence of complement binding donor epitope sharing antibody in the kidney of the recipient.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a kidney transplant patient had a complement-binding donor specific HLA epitope sharing antibody that was responsible for a severe antibody-mediated rejection episode.

we found that donor-specific antibodies (DSA) in kidney transplant recipients can bind to complement proteins and that these complement-binding antibodies can be found in patients with acute antibody-mediated rejection and in patients without rejection.
we have shown that complement-binding antibodies (CBAs) can be detected in kidney transplant recipients.
The main takeaway from our work is that
complement-binding donor epitope-specific antibodies can be present in kidney recipients.
we identified a donor-specific antibody that bound complement and was associated with acute antibody-mediated rejection.

the presence of donor epitope sharing complement binding antibodies (CES-CBA) in the recipient is associated with a higher rate of acute rejection (AR) and worse renal function in kidney transplant recipients.
